scenes.tts: How can a cell make a reaction run uphill without breaking thermodynamics? Watch what happens when glucose receives a phosphate. At cellular concentrations, glucose plus free phosphate favors the starting side. Its actual delta G is positive, so the cart rolls backward.

scenes.visual: Use one full-frame world carried through the film: a broad schematic hill, labelled SCHEMATIC, fills 70% of the frame height. Before the first word, a large cart labelled 'glucose + Pi' is already climbing from lower left toward a gold target block labelled 'G6P' at upper right. During the first question the wheels turn and the cart loses speed; during 'favors the starting side' a balance arrow tilts left; during 'positive' a large ΔG gauge beside the hill rises above zero in red; during 'rolls backward' the cart rolls visibly to its starting mark while small track markers continue drifting past. Draw only labelled blocks and carts, no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: How can a cell make a reaction run uphill without breaking thermodynamics? Watch what happens when glucose receives a phosphate. At cellular concentrations, glucose plus free phosphate favors the starting side. Its actual ΔG is positive, so the cart rolls backward.

scenes.visual: Keep the same hill and cart dimly visible and moving slowly in the background. Center the title 'How cells pull reactions uphill' for two seconds, then lift it away as the ΔG gauge brightens for the next scene.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule that governs every case. A reaction runs forward only when its actual delta G is negative. Enzymes lower activation barriers and speed traffic. They cannot change the sign of delta G. The cell must change the chemical journey or the concentrations along it.
scenes.caption: Here is the rule that governs every case. A reaction runs forward only when its actual ΔG is negative. Enzymes lower activation barriers and speed traffic. They cannot change the sign of ΔG. The cell must change the chemical journey or the concentrations along it.
scenes.visual: Carry the hill forward at the same scale. On 'runs forward' the cart advances only while the adjacent actual-ΔG gauge is below zero in green; when the needle crosses above zero, the cart reverses. On 'Enzymes' a large enzyme gate labelled 'enzyme' lowers a tall schematic activation hump and carts pass faster, while fixed start and finish flags do not move. On 'cannot change the sign' the gate pulses but the ΔG needle stays positive and the cart still returns. On the final sentence, the single track forks briefly into two ghosted options labelled 'joined chemistry' and 'change concentrations'; moving arrows travel along both.
scenes.narration: Here is the rule that governs every case. A reaction runs forward only when its actual ΔG is negative. Enzymes lower activation barriers and speed traffic. They cannot change the sign of ΔG. The cell must change the chemical journey or the concentrations along it.

scenes.tts: In simplest form, the cell ties an uphill reaction to a downhill one. Hexokinase directly transfers A T P's end phosphoryl to glucose, not through free phosphate. A T P becomes A D P as glucose becomes glucose-six-phosphate. This is one chemical reaction, so the free-energy changes add. Its actual delta G is negative, and the joined carts move forward.
scenes.caption: In simplest form, the cell ties an uphill reaction to a downhill one. Hexokinase directly transfers ATP's end phosphoryl to glucose, not through free phosphate. ATP becomes ADP as glucose becomes glucose-6-phosphate. This is one chemical reaction, so the free-energy changes add. Its actual ΔG is negative, and the joined carts move forward.
scenes.visual: Transform the carried hill into two connected slopes without cutting away. A light cart labelled 'glucose' faces uphill on the left; a heavier cart labelled 'ATP' faces a steeper downhill track on the right. A thick rope passes through one large block labelled 'hexokinase' between them. During 'directly transfers', a gold badge labelled 'phosphoryl' travels through the hexokinase block from the ATP cart to the glucose cart; no free Pi block appears. As the badge lands, labels morph simultaneously from ATP to ADP and glucose to G6P. During 'changes add', two animated arrows merge into one green net arrow and the actual-ΔG gauge drops below zero. The rope stays taut and both carts keep moving forward through the final words. Label the whole picture SCHEMATIC.

ATP becomes ADP as glucose becomes glucose-6-phosphate. This is one chemical reaction, so the free-energy changes add. Its actual ΔG is negative, and the joined carts move forward.

scenes.tts: Now predict what happens if a mutant enzyme separates the jobs. One site hydrolyzes A T P. Another site tries to attach free phosphate to glucose, with no shared intermediate or conformational link. The standard free-energy changes still add on paper. Will glucose-six-phosphate form?
scenes.caption: Now predict what happens if a mutant enzyme separates the jobs. One site hydrolyzes ATP. Another site tries to attach free phosphate to glucose, with no shared intermediate or conformational link. The standard free-energy changes still add on paper. Will glucose-6-phosphate form?
scenes.visual: Keep the same hill and carts. On 'separates', split the hexokinase block into two widely separated blocks and let the rope fall loose between them. At the downhill block, ATP and a water droplet icon enter and ADP plus Pi blocks begin to emerge. At the uphill block, separate glucose and Pi blocks nudge toward a G6P target and hover there, outcome not yet shown. On 'add on paper', a small arithmetic card shows a green negative sum while a red broken-link symbol remains between the sites. On the final question, enlarge 'Will glucose-6-phosphate form?' across the upper third; the carts continue a gentle two-way rocking motion.
scenes.narration: Now predict what happens if a mutant enzyme separates the jobs. One site hydrolyzes ATP. Another site tries to attach free phosphate to glucose, with no shared intermediate or conformational link. The standard free-energy changes still add on paper. Will glucose-6-phosphate form?

scenes.visual: Hold the full question 'Will glucose-6-phosphate form?' for 4.5 seconds over the separated sites. A four-dot thinking indicator fills one dot per second; the loose rope sways slightly and both carts rock in place without revealing a product.

scenes.tts: No. A T P hydrolysis runs downhill, but its free energy leaves as heat. The glucose cart still rolls backward. Arithmetic alone is not coupling. Chemistry must be joined by direct transfer, a shared intermediate, or linked shape changes.
scenes.caption: No. ATP hydrolysis runs downhill, but its free energy leaves as heat. The glucose cart still rolls backward. Arithmetic alone is not coupling. Chemistry must be joined by direct transfer, a shared intermediate, or linked shape changes.
scenes.visual: On 'No', stamp a clear red NO beside the uphill site. The ATP cart rolls down and changes to ADP while expanding heat-wave lines drift away; simultaneously the glucose cart rolls back to its start. Tear the arithmetic card in half on 'not coupling'. During the three joining mechanisms, rebuild the connector in the same central position three ways in sequence: a gold badge crossing directly, a labelled intermediate block carried across, then two meshed protein-shape gears turning together. Keep at most one version visible at a time, and finish with the direct-transfer rope taut between the carts.
scenes.narration: No. ATP hydrolysis runs downhill, but its free energy leaves as heat. The glucose cart still rolls backward. Arithmetic alone is not coupling. Chemistry must be joined by direct transfer, a shared intermediate, or linked shape changes.

scenes.tts: Cells also change concentrations. Here, A to B plus C has standard delta G plus twenty-one kilojoules per mole. B to D has minus thirty-four. Draining B pulls the first step's actual delta G below zero. Although the pathway total is minus thirteen, that is not enough. Every step carrying forward flux must have negative actual delta G.
scenes.caption: Cells also change concentrations. Here, A → B + C has ΔG°' = +21 kJ/mol. B → D has ΔG°' = −34 kJ/mol. Draining B pulls the first step's actual ΔG below zero. Although the pathway total is −13 kJ/mol, that is not enough. Every step carrying forward flux must have negative actual ΔG.
scenes.visual: Transform the same hill tracks into a large schematic pathway A → B + C → D spanning the frame. Label the first rise '+21 kJ/mol standard' and the second drop '−34 kJ/mol standard'; animate the two labels combining into a smaller badge 'pathway total −13'. B is a basin of large blue beads. During 'Draining B', the second enzyme wheel turns continuously and carries B beads into a D chute faster than the first step supplies them. As B falls, a separate actual-ΔG gauge for the first step crosses below zero and A carts begin moving forward. On 'not enough', briefly stop the drain: B beads pile up, the first-step gauge reaches zero, and A carts stop despite the negative pathway-total badge. Restart the drain for the final rule so every forward arrow glows green only beside a negative actual-ΔG gauge.
scenes.narration: Cells also change concentrations. Here, A → B + C has ΔG°' = +21 kJ/mol. B → D has ΔG°' = −34 kJ/mol. Draining B pulls the first step's actual ΔG below zero. Although the pathway total is −13 kJ/mol, that is not enough. Every step carrying forward flux must have negative actual ΔG.

scenes.tts: Take a separate standard example. Coupling to A T P shifts K from about one-thousandth to about two hundred sixty-seven. That moves equilibrium toward products by more than two hundred thousand-fold.
scenes.caption: Take a separate standard example. Coupling to ATP shifts K from about 0.001 to about 267. That moves equilibrium toward products by more than 200,000-fold.
scenes.visual: Preserve the joined hill, but relabel the uphill cart 'A → B' and add a small tag 'separate example, not glucose' (glucose's own K goes from 0.0038 to 840, so the glucose label must not sit beside these K values). Transform the ΔG gauge into a large computed standard-K'eq dial at the hill's base. During 'one-thousandth', the pointer rests at K = 0.001 and one product bead sits opposite a much larger reactant tray. As 'two hundred sixty-seven' is spoken, the ATP rope pulls, the pointer sweeps to K = 267, and beads stream continuously into the product tray. On 'more than two hundred thousand-fold', a counter rolls from ×1 to >×200,000 while the product tray fills most of the frame. Label the dial COMPUTED FROM STATED K VALUES; do not draw molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Take a separate standard example. Coupling to ATP shifts K from about 0.001 to about 267. That moves equilibrium toward products by more than 200,000-fold.

scenes.tts: That is the answer to our puzzle. Hexokinase's direct phosphoryl transfer changes the journey, so glucose phosphorylation can run forward. A following step may instead keep a product scarce. The same rule governs A T P and other activated carriers. Uphill chemistry runs only when coupling makes its actual delta G negative.

Then, on the A → B + C → D track beside it (relabel that cart 'A', never 'glucose'), show the moving B-drain belt keeping that uphill cart flowing; do not show a drain belt pulling the glucose + Pi cart. During the last sentence, the moving hill world dims behind the centered line 'Uphill chemistry runs only when coupling makes its actual ΔG negative.'; underline 'actual ΔG negative' as the cart reaches the product side.
